bound by cessation,
do not sever their afflictions.
Having given rise to overweening pride,
he subsequently employs the power of his knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*) to instruct sentient beings,
causing them to sever their afflictions and achieve ultimate exhaustion of outflows. This concludes this section.
Next, based on the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*),
transformation is initiated. Within this sequence of gates,
one first contemplates the ultimate truth by means of the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
Next, one uses the power of karma to contemplate the various karmas performed by householders,
thereby causing them to cultivate pure karma;
next, one uses the power of meditative concentration to contemplate those who have left the home life.
He causes them to cultivate the practice of meditative concentration.
Subsequently, by means of the powers of the faculties up to the power of the exhaustion of outflows,
he brings all sentient beings to liberation from suffering and delivers them by means of the Path.
The sequence therein is the same as in the first gate; these two gates are concluded.
Third, the manifestation of transformation arises from the wisdom of the dharma-realm of dependent origination.
What is the sequence?
The existence of the dharmas of the dharma-realm of dependent origination is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
the emptiness of these dharmic characteristics is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Free from both existence and non-existence,
within the *tathāgatagarbha*, there are dharmas exceeding the sands of the Ganges;
through the manifestation of the characteristics of dependent origination, these are termed the *dharmadhātu* of dependent origination.
Within this, one first contemplates the dharma-realm of dependent origination by means of the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*),
and subsequently by means of the power of karma (*karma-bala*).
Observing sentient beings in the world performing such karma and receiving such fruits,
he next employs his power of meditative concentration to manifest three kinds of appearances for the sake of suffering beings.
And he instructs them, causing them to give rise to faith and understanding;
subsequently, by means of the powers of the faculties up to the power of the destruction of the outflows.
By means of the Way, they are delivered and liberated,
causing them to emerge from all sufferings;
the sequence therein is the same as that of the initial gate.
The sequence is as follows.
Next is the seventh gate,
which consists of the twofold classification of the gates of conversion and instruction.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
the first two powers are the power of conversion.
The latter eight powers are the power of instruction;
they universally proclaim cause and effect and provide guidance to sentient beings.
Causing others to give rise to faith and understanding is called the power of transformation;
it clarifies and manifests one's conduct and demeanor.
Pointing out the mind’s deviousness and bestowing instructions so as to cause the arousal of practice and cultivation is called the power of instruction.
Among the first two powers, the first—
the power of the possible and the impossible—
is for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Causing them to distance themselves from inverted views regarding cause and effect;
this is the second karmic power:
the teaching and transformation of sentient beings.
It causes one to remain far removed from the views of no cause and no effect.
Among the latter eight powers, the first four powers consist of knowing the objects and the mental faculties.
Regarding the four subsequent methods of bestowing the Dharma, among those four,
the beginner seeker knows that they are seeking [the Dharma].
What is this mind? It is what is called meditative concentration (dhyāna).
For what reason is it called "mind"?
By means of abiding in concentration,
its outward functions are stilled;
because these functions are stilled and it returns to its essence, the mind is called "mind" (citta).
Because the mind inclines toward the Dharma, it is called "seeking.
Other types of seeking are likewise so named.
Why, then, is the mind specifically clarified here?
As Nāgārjuna said:
"The wisdom within a distracted mind is incapable of entering the Dharma."
Just as colored pigments without glue will not adhere to an object,
one must rely on a concentrated mind to be capable of entering the Dharma; therefore,
it is necessary to clarify the mind.
For what reason is the concentrated mind explained first?
The sutras state that it is not fixed;
this is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
In the textual passage of the *Ekottarika-āgama*,
it is only after the discussion of the powers of nature (*dharmatā-bala*) that concentration (*samādhi*) is subsequently explained.
This is the scriptural text of the *Ekottarika*.
The explanation will be given later in the section on the "Destinations.
Generally, in various sūtras, these are taught before the faculties and powers.
There are two interpretations for this.
First, according to my own interpretation:
the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) before they give rise to transformative activity (*nirmāṇa*).
Therefore, concentration is explained first.
Second, this is explained in terms of the sentient beings to be converted:
among the five faculties of sentient beings,
wisdom is the primary one.
The Venerable Śrīlāta previously explained meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because of the sequential order of the topics, he first clarified the mind (*citta*).
As for "those who seek by means of the two faculties":
One seeks through the faculty of knowledge. What is this faculty?
It refers to faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and so forth.
Why are they called faculties (*indriya*)?
This is explained as before:
they are brought to completion through prior cultivation.
Because they are able to produce what follows,
they are called "roots" (indriya).
For what reason are the roots explained?
Since one who lacks the roots cannot enter when being granted the Dharma-teachings,
it is necessary to clarify the roots.
For what reason are the roots explained next?
There are two meanings to this "explanation.
First, in contrast to the previous interpretation,
it refers to the five sense faculties.
With wisdom as the primary factor,
wisdom is explained after meditative concentration;
because this is the sequential order of their meanings, the faculties are clarified next.
The second pair is explained as follows:
the faculties are already established,
while desire arises in the present.
Since that which is established first must precede, the faculties (indriya) are explained next.
Regarding those who seek through aspiration, one knows them as seekers through aspiration.
What is this aspiration?
It refers to the mind of aspiration.
Why is it called "aspiration" (*prārthanā*)?
Because the aspiring mind seeks the Dharma, it is called aspiration.
For what reason is clear aspiration required?
Because one wishes to bestow the Dharma of the Path, yet without desire there is no taking;
therefore, clear aspiration is necessary.
For what reason is aspiration explained next?
There are two interpretations.
First, it is explained in contrast to the preceding [section].
The faculties are established first;
desire arises subsequently. Therefore, the faculties are mentioned first, and desire is spoken of later.
Because it follows the sequence of the meanings, the aspiration is explained next.
Second, in contrast to the subsequent understanding,
one first seeks within the Dharma.
This is what is called desire.
When one habituates to desire without reforming,
it finally becomes one's nature.
In the preceding section on the nature [of craving], desire (*kāma*) was explained; because of the sequential order of the meanings, aspiration (*prārthanā*) is now clarified next.
Regarding the four types of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*), one should understand that "seeking" refers to the seeker (*paryeṣaka*).
What are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?
They are of the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*). Why are they called "latent dispositions"?
Their nature is that of afflictions;
because they bind individuals according to their circumstances, they are called "latent tendencies" (anuśaya).
For what reason are these latent tendencies clarified?
This is because one wishes to prescribe the appropriate remedy according to the specific affliction.
Why is this explained next?
There are two meanings to "understanding" (or "liberation").
The preceding pair of verses explain that because one continues to practice desire without reforming it,
it subsequently becomes the nature of an "affliction" (anuśaya).
Regarding desire, the subsequent explanation clarifies the application of knowledge;
this is explained in two pairs.
First, one must know the illness.
Thereafter, one administers the medicine.
For this reason, prior to reaching that destination, one must clearly understand the nature of the motivating factors (*saṃskāra*).
The four powers mentioned above consist of knowing the mental capacities of sentient beings;
the four powers below consist of bestowing the Dharma.
Among these, the first bestows the methods of phenomena,
causing all sentient beings to find peace of mind within those phenomena.
With his knowledge of past lives and divine eye,
he bestowed upon them the principles of the Dharma,
causing them to enter into the Middle Way.
Finally, for the one whose outflows were exhausted,
he conferred the dharma of fruition,
causing him to reach ultimate perfection.
In the beginning and middle, because the afflictions of sentient beings differ according to their dispositions,
one instructs them by means of the five perfections (*pañcapāramitā*).
For sentient beings with excessive greed:
Teach the contemplation of impurity to those with much anger, and teach the cultivation of loving-kindness and compassion to those with much anger.
A question is asked:
Greed and anger are afflictions of the desire realm that are directly contrary to meditative concentration;
one who has attained dhyāna-nirvāṇa (meditative absorption) will necessarily be free from these faults.
Through the power of meditative concentration directed forward,
one knows the concentrated mind of another;
that is, one who possesses a concentrated mind.
Since you have already abandoned greed and hatred,
why do you now say that those with much greed should be taught to contemplate impurity,
and those with much hatred should be taught to cultivate loving-kindness and compassion?
The commentary states:
Although ordinary persons attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*),
they merely suppress the coarse manifestations [of afflictions].
His innate tendencies still remain;
therefore, he is instructed by this teaching.
Furthermore, due to the power of his prior concentration.
Taking concentration as primary is called the power of concentration; therein,
one also discerns those who lack a concentrated mind and those who possess a concentrated mind.
Although greed and hatred may not exist [in some], they do exist in others; therefore,
this teaching involves the contemplation of the gateway of impurity and so forth.
For those with a preponderance of delusion, one teaches the contemplation of causes and conditions.
A question is asked:
"Since śrāvakas have dull faculties, they are taught to contemplate the Four Noble Truths."
Those of the Śrāvaka vehicle are not taught to contemplate causes and conditions; those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle possess sharp faculties and are taught to contemplate causes and conditions.
Why, then, is it said here that those with much ignorance are taught to contemplate causes and conditions?
The commentary states:
There are two kinds of ignorance (*moha*).
First, dullness and lack of knowledge.
To be like cattle or sheep, lacking any discernment,
is called ignorance.
Those of the second capacity possess sharp and keen faculties, yet they falsely establish conceptual constructs.
To be deluded regarding the causes, conditions, and fruits is called ignorance (*moha*).
What is now termed "ignorance" is taught as a contemplation on the meaning of causes and conditions; it shall be addressed in a later section.
Although it is named ignorance, its nature is actually sharp and discerning.
Therefore, the teaching on dependent origination instructs one to contemplate past ignorance, formations, and so forth,
enabling one to understand past causes and thereby abandon the view of causelessness.
He teaches the contemplation of future birth, aging, death, and so forth,
causing them to know the subsequent results and thereby abandon the view that there is no result.
He teaches the contemplation of present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth.
He knows both cause and effect.
A question is asked:

"Previously, in the context of the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*) as well as the power of karma (*karma-bala*), you have already taught [the principles of] cause and effect."
Now, this teaching on causes and conditions is intended to make one understand cause and effect;
how does it differ from what was stated previously?
The explanation says:

"These are thus for the sake of transformation."
This is not called a fault. Question:
The previous explanation that the three types of karma are without fault is already sufficient in its meaning.
Why is it necessary to further state that the three types of action follow wisdom?
The treatise says:
"There is no fault in what was previously stated regarding the three types of action."
It was not yet clear for what reason this lack of error is attained;
now it is clarified that it is attained by following the movement of wisdom.
To "know the three periods of time without obstruction" means:
The Buddha possesses unimpeded knowledge regarding all matters throughout the three periods of time.
A question is asked:
"The past has already ceased and is no longer present; the future has not yet come into being; and the present does not abide."
How can it be said that the Buddha penetrates the three periods of time?
The explanation is:
although the past has already ceased, [the Buddha knows it].
It is not that they have never existed;
they will exist in the future and are conventionally existent in the present.
Therefore, the Buddha knows them.
Question: It was previously stated that wisdom is undiminished and there is nothing it does not know.
Why is it necessary to further state that it knows the three periods of time?
The commentary states:
Regarding the previous statement that wisdom does not diminish,
it means that there is no deficiency in the thorough penetration of the general characteristics of all phenomena.
This explains that one’s comprehension of the three periods of time is unimpeded;
therefore, it is stated once again.
The analysis of its characteristics is thus.
Next is the second section, which distinguishes and determines what is correct and incorrect.
Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), there are three different explanations.
The first explanation is as previously stated.
The second is that which was taught by Kātyāyanīputra:
the ten powers (*daśabala*) and four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) of the Tathāgata constitute fourteen [factors].
The fifteen [aspects] of Great Compassion, combined with the three applications of mindfulness,
total eighteen. This one interpretation was refuted by Nāgārjuna.
Because this was stated,
it is called the teaching of Kātyāyanīputra;
if it were the teaching of the Śākya-son (the Buddha), it would not be thus.
The virtues of the Buddha are like the ocean—
immeasurable and boundless. Why, then,
do you further speak of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and so forth as his unique qualities?
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas are likewise able to know what is possible and what is impossible, up to the exhaustion of the outflows."
How is it that the proclamation of the qualities of the ten powers is designated as an uncommon attribute?
It is asked:
If one says that the qualities of the ten powers are not uncommon because they are not within the scope of other persons, [how so?]
The two vehicles also possess a small portion of such qualities as the absence of physical error;
why, then, are they called the "unshared dharmas" (āveṇika-dharma)?
The treatise itself explains: [as follows].
I do not teach that the absence of physical errors and so forth constitutes the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Rather, I teach that the body and so forth are eternally free from error as the unique qualities.
Therefore, these are absent in Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there is another explanation:
first, the Tathāgata possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*),
and that which he knows is vast and extensive.
Second, they are endowed with immeasurable merit;
third, they are endowed with great compassion;
fourth, they possess mastery over wisdom.
Five is unimpeded mastery regarding all that is to be known;
six is mastery over meditative concentration;
and seven is mastery over transformation.
Seventh, he is able to bestow immeasurable predictions of enlightenment;
eighth, his predictions are never in vain;
ninth, his speech is without error.
Tenth, his wisdom does not diminish,
and he does not regress in what is to be known.
Eleventh, he constantly practices the mind of equanimity.
Twelfth is knowing the proper time and the improper time;
that is, knowing the time when sentient beings should receive transformation,
as well as knowing the time when sentient beings are not yet ready for transformation.
Thirteen, his mindfulness is without lapse.
Fourteen, he is free from the habitual tendencies of affliction.
Fifteen, no one is able to legitimately point out any fault in him.
Sixteenth, no one is able to see the crown of his head.
Seventeenth, the soles of his feet are soft and supple;
any sentient being who encounters them immediately attains happiness.
Eighteenth, they attain the power of supernatural faculties (abhijñā),
transforming the minds of sentient beings so that they may be easily converted and delivered. This is the eighteenth.
Regarding this one teaching,
even Nāgārjuna did not say it; furthermore,
this is not a teaching found within the Tripiṭaka.
This refers to the words of praise for the Buddha compiled from the sūtras by various śrāvaka masters, which constitute these eighteen qualities:
his speech is without error, his mindfulness is without lapse, his wisdom does not diminish, and he constantly practices equanimity.
This is taken as the subject of discourse from among the uncommon dharmas of the Mahāyāna.
The mark of the invisible crown of the head and the softness of the soles of the feet are among the Buddha’s marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
If these are described as the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma),
they are not limited to many;
why stop at eighteen?
Among these three explanations,
the first is correct,
while the latter two are incorrect.
It is not so. Next, its essential nature is distinguished through three gates,
within which there are four sub-gates of analysis.
First, the classification according to the three natures— wholesome, unwholesome,
and indeterminate— as taught by Nāgārjuna:
the essential nature of the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) is exclusively wholesome.
Second, the distinction between those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*). As Nāgārjuna stated:
"The essence of the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) is exclusively without outflows."
Third, regarding the distinction between merit and wisdom,
the treatises state that it is indeterminate;
this is spoken from the perspective of the primary factor.
The eighteen unshared attributes (āveṇika-dharma) consist solely of wisdom.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
"In the Mahāyāna, the eighteen unshared attributes are taught."
All things take wisdom as their essential meaning;
since wisdom is the sovereign,
it is called "insight" (prajñā).
When categorized according to their specific characteristics, they are subsumed under two gates: the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*) and wisdom (*jñāna*).
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
It is taught that the wisdom and merit of the Tathāgata constitute the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*),
whereas the natural marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) as their karmic retribution are not said to be unique qualities.
Among the eighteen [unique qualities],...
Knowing no limit to wisdom, knowing no decrease in insight,
and thoroughly comprehending the three periods of time—
these six constitute wisdom.
The remainder are meritorious qualities;
this is also acceptable.
Furthermore, the essential nature of wisdom and liberation within the first six [liberations] and the liberation of one who has attained knowledge (prajñā-vimukti) is as follows.
This is wisdom;
the remainder are meritorious qualities.
These four are distinguished according to the five aggregates of the Tathāgata.
Among the eighteen [dhātus],
the absence of error in body and speech, as well as bodily and vocal actions that proceed in accordance with wisdom—
these four constitute the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
The absence of divergent thoughts is its aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
The absence of an unconcentrated mind should be its aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
Yet, the treatise refers to it as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

This is because, within meditative concentration, its functional activity ceases and it is described as consciousness from the perspective of its essence; it does not mean that one is actually discussing the state of concentration itself.
The remainder constitutes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is omitted for brevity;
such is the nature of their essential character.
Next, regarding the fourth gate,
which distinguishes [the elements] by way of location,
there are two explanations in the treatise.
One school asserts that these eighteen [attributes] exist in the fourth dhyāna,
because when the Buddha attained enlightenment, he realized bodhi while in the fourth dhyāna.
A second school asserts that they consist of the absence of faults in body and speech.
The body and speech follow wisdom;
they are subsumed within the five stages of the desire and form realms.
These five stages consist of the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
The remaining unshared dharmas (āveṇika-dharma) pervade and are subsumed within all three realms and nine stages.
The eight dhyānas of the desire realm constitute these nine stages.
The analysis of the bases is thus.
Next, the fivefold classification of the three types of action:
as for bodily action, that which is free from error and wherein the body follows the movement of wisdom is bodily action.
The absence of error in verbal action and speech that accords with wisdom constitute verbal karma;
all other unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) are mental karma.
Such are the three types of karma.
Next is the sixth section: the analysis of the four conditions.
As stated in the treatise:
"The absence of error in body and speech, as well as bodily and vocal actions that follow wisdom, are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*)."
It arises from only two conditions,
namely the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
because it is not a mental factor (*citta-dharma*).
They do not arise from object conditions or sequential conditions;
the remaining fourteen mental factors and qualities arise by way of all four conditions.
Arising from the perfuming of past virtuous karma is dependent origination by way of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The sequential arising of mental phenomena is dependent origination by way of the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Arising by taking an object as its condition is dependent origination by way of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The eighteen unshared qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) arise from superior conditions; all phenomena do not obstruct them.
This is a brief summary.

222. The Meaning of the One Hundred and Forty Unique Qualities (End of Part 20). Section Three: A Detailed Analysis of the Characteristics of the One Hundred and Forty Unique Qualities through Three Gates. I. The Performance of Action; II. Subsumption under the Common Characteristics of the Eighteen Unique Qualities; III. First, the Detailed Analysis of Characteristics.
The one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
These are the merits of the Tathāgata as set forth in the *Bhūmivastu-śāstra* (Treatise on the Support of the Stages).
The "unshared dharmas" (āveṇika-dharma), which do not share names with those below, are divided into two categories:
first, in relation to ordinary beings; second, in relation to followers of the Two Vehicles.
The difference between existence and non-existence is called "unshared" (āveṇika).
Furthermore, the distinction between the fulfillment and non-fulfillment of these two [qualities] in relation to bodhisattvas is also called "unshared."
The *Guanglun* (Extensive Treatise) on the qualities [of the Buddha] is immeasurable and unique; here,
we shall explain one hundred and forty based on a single gateway.
What are their names?
They are the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of a Tathāgata;
together, these constitute one hundred and twelve dharmas.
The four types of universal purity combined result in one hundred and sixteen dharmas.
When the ten powers are added to these,
there are one hundred and twenty-six.
Adding the four fearlessnesses makes one hundred and thirty;
great compassion is one; and the two forms of non-forgetfulness of the Dharma are two.
Adding the three applications of mindfulness and the three forms of self-protection makes eight in total;
including the elimination of all habitual tendencies, there are nine.
The tenth is the sublime wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Together with the preceding one hundred and forty unique qualities, these constitute the one hundred and forty unique dharmas (*āveṇikadharma*).
Such is the enumeration.
Now, I shall explain them in sequence according to their respective categories:
the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics,
as well as the qualities of physical form and appearance, will be discussed together in one section.
The outward manifestation of merit is called a "mark" (lakṣaṇa);
furthermore, that which expresses inner virtue is also called a mark.
It is graceful, lovely, and pleasing.
To accord with human sentiments is called "goodness";
to discern these marks of excellence is called "discrimination."
Briefly, there are three sections:
first, clarifying its fruit;
second, discerning its cause.
The three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) are that which is cultivated through practice.
Within the results of this higher knowledge, there are five specific sections.
First, the formal enumeration and exposition.
Second, the extent of the two concentrations;
third, the discussion of the real and the responsive;
fourth, clarifying the locus of attainment.
Five: Distinguishing Superiority and Inferiority.
First, the formal distinction and enumeration: What are these thirty-two marks?
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, [the marks are]:
first, the soles of the feet are level and even like the bottom of a casket;
second, there are thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the feet.
Third, his fingers are slender and long.
Fourth, his heels are broad.
Fifth, his hands and feet have webbed membranes like those of the king of white geese.
Sixth, his hands and feet are soft and supple.
Seventh, his calves are like those of the king of the eneya deer.
Eighth, the bones of his ankles do not protrude.
Ninth, when standing upright, his hands reach his knees.
Tenth, his male organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a horse-king.
Eleventh, his body is perfectly proportioned like a nyagrodha tree.
12. The hairs on his body point upward.
13. Each hair curls to the right.
14. His body is golden in color.
The halo of the Buddha is fifteen feet in circumference and one fathom in width. This refers to Śākyamuni;
for other Buddhas, the distance of their bodily radiance is not fixed.
Sixteenth, his skin is fine and soft, such that dust and grime do not adhere to it.
Seventeenth, seven parts of his body—the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck—are well-rounded and full.
Eighteenth, his upper body is like that of a lion.
Nineteenth, his upper arms and elbows are rounded and full.
Twentieth, his collarbones are complete and his body is straight and upright.
Twenty-first, he has forty teeth. Twenty-second, [he has] forty teeth.
Twenty-three: his teeth are even and closely set.
Twenty-four: his teeth are white and pure.
Twenty-five: his jaw is square like that of a lion.
Twenty-sixth, he attains the supreme sense of taste in succession.
Twenty-seventh, the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of his head and the invisible crown together constitute a single mark.
Twenty-eighth, his tongue is broad and long.
29. A voice like that of Brahmā;
30. Eyes of deep blue color; 31.
Eyelids that blink up and down like those of a bull king.
The thirty-second is the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
Such are the names of the thirty-two marks.
What are the eighty secondary characteristics?
As stated in the *Bhūmisaṃvara-sūtra*:
"The twenty fingers of the hands and feet are all exquisitely beautiful;
these constitute the twenty [marks]."
The eight areas—the palms of both hands, the soles of both feet, and the surfaces and backs of both hands and both feet—are flat and full.
Together with the preceding [thirty-two marks], these constitute twenty-eight secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). These include:

the two heels, the two knees, the two thighs, the two shoulders, the two elbows, the two wrists, the two shanks, the two buttocks, the mark of the male organ being concealed, the two circles (the *ūrṇā* between the eyebrows and the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown), the two upper arms, the two sides of the torso, the two armpits, the two breasts, the waist, the back, the heart, the abdomen, and the throat.
All are exquisitely beautiful,
numbering thirty-two; when combined with the preceding [marks], they constitute sixty kinds of secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
These sixty marks below the throat constitute the [next] set;
his upper and lower teeth are all exquisitely beautiful,
which counts as two.
The two lips, the two gums, the two cheeks, the two temples, the two eyes, the two ears, the two eyebrows, the two nostrils, and the two corners of the forehead—
all are exquisitely beautiful.
This constitutes another ten.
Combined with the preceding [marks], these constitute twenty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
These are the twenty secondary marks from the throat upward;
thus, they total eighty.
The primary marks and secondary signs are thus;
this concludes the first section. Next, the second section distinguishes their number. Question:
Do these marks and signs cease with these [thirty-two], or are there more?
As stated in the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks" (*Lakṣaṇasāgara-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
regarding the locations of the aforementioned thirty-two marks:
Each of these possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of merit.
The names of these various marks and signs are distinct throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The merit, karmic actions, and benefits are also distinct.
Although these characteristics exist,
they are subtle and difficult to perceive.
It is like the jewel atop the head of the Brahma King named Indrā,
which none of the gods can see;
it is also like that king of wish-fulfilling jewels.
This jewel possesses immeasurable power.
While the form of the jewel can be seen,
the efficacy of its power cannot be perceived.
Such are the marks of a Buddha.
The coarse marks of the transformation body can be beheld with the eyes.
Regarding his true virtues and wondrous marks,
no humans or devas are able to see them;
only great bodhisattvas can.
The Buddha alone has reached the ultimate understanding; he possesses complete knowledge and vision, whereas others perceive only a small portion.
This is solely for the purpose of transforming and delivering śrāvakas and ordinary worldlings.
We have merely spoken here of the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
A question is asked:
The sutras state that within the Tathāgata’s chest there is a mark of a golden *vajra* in the form of a ten-thousand-character diagram (*wanzi*).
It is named "Incomparable.
Why was its name not included among the previous thirty-two?
This is because it is encompassed within the ocean of numerous marks.
Therefore, they are not listed among the thirty-two [marks].
Such is the conclusion of these two gates regarding the number [of marks].
Next, the third gate distinguishes and determines the True and the Responsive [Bodies].
Question: Regarding the merits of the primary and secondary marks mentioned above, are they real or are they manifested?
There are two ways of distinguishing them.
A pair of subtle bodies that transcend all marks can manifest the thirty-two major signs and eighty minor marks;
their appearance in royal palaces and birth therein are all termed "response."
Because it is an emanation (*nirmāṇakāya*), it ultimately returns to extinction.
Second, regarding the manifested thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics,
they are analyzed according to their meaning as being both real (*dharmakāya*) and emanated (*nirmāṇakāya*).
That which arises from one's own karma is called "true. Therefore,
in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages),
these marks and signs are termed the "Body of True Retribution" (*sambhogakāya*).
These very marks and signs manifest differently— whether refined or coarse— according to the various sentient beings;
appearing or ceasing in this way, they are called "the Responsive" (nirmāṇakāya).
This is truly because the Real and the Responsive are inseparable;

thus, the body that manifests birth is eternally unborn, and the body that manifests extinction is likewise unextinguished. Since this is the case regarding both birth and extinction, [so it is with all phenomena].
The principles regarding the large and small, the refined and the coarse, are likewise the same.
The True and the Responsive should be understood in this manner; thus concludes the third gate.
Next is the fourth gate.
To clarify the locus of attainment:
as the causes confronted differ, the loci of attainment likewise vary.
If one confronts the wholesome karma cultivated prior to the stages (bhūmi), [the result is attained accordingly].
From the Stage of the Pure Mind onward, the marks and signs arise as a result of maturation.
If contrasted with the causes cultivated on the [ten] stages,
they arise as maturation sequentially according to each stage.
These two meanings are as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*.
Thus concludes the fourth gate concerning the attainment of the locus.
The fifth section in sequence distinguishes and determines their relative superiority and inferiority,
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (Dichizhi).
The accumulation of merit and virtue of all sentient beings, once returned to the Buddha,

is equal to the merit and virtue accumulated in a single pore-mark of the Tathāgata; the accumulation of merit and virtue in all his pore-marks is likewise [equal to the merit of all sentient beings].
The accumulation of merit from all the secondary physical marks (anuvyañjana) of that Tathāgata, increased a hundredfold,
equals one primary mark (lakṣaṇa).
Thus, one obtains a single mark;
excluding the mark of the white tuft of hair, the mark of the fleshly protuberance on the crown, and the mark of the Brahma-voice—
setting aside these three marks.
One attains the remaining marks.
By accumulating the merit of all other marks and increasing it a thousandfold,
one attains the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
When the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* mark increases a hundred-thousandfold,
one attains the *uṣṇīṣa* and the mark of the invisible crown of the head.
When the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* mark increases a hundred-thousand times ten millionfold, [one attains the mark of the invisible crown].
He thus attains the Tathāgata’s mark of the conch-shell sound;
for this reason, the Tathāgata emits sounds at will with a pure Brahma-voice.
Extending even to the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions,
such an accumulation of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable and boundless merits is inconceivable.
The preceding section has clarified the fruit of the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana).
Next, the second section clarifies the causes for the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).
The sūtra explains the causes for the primary marks but does not discuss the causes for the secondary signs.
Regarding the analysis of the causes of manifestation,
there is a fourfold classification.
First, the formal determination of the causes.
Second, distinguishing according to their respective positions;
third, clarifying that these causes, being immeasurable, are capable of producing the primary and secondary marks;
fourth, clarifying the differences between what is taught in the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
In the correct analysis of causes,
there are three distinct categories of meaning.
The first is the specific cause (*viśeṣa-hetu*).
Second is the cause of loss;
third is the pervasive cause.
As for what is called the specific cause:
The causes for attaining each of the thirty-two marks are distinct,
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (Dizhi):
[they consist of] upholding the precepts, patience, and generosity.
Therefore, one attains level and stable soles of the feet,
as described in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
One maintains the precepts with immovability.
With a mind of generosity that does not waver and abiding securely in truthful speech,
one attains level soles on the feet.
By making offerings to one's parents, preceptors, and elders,
and by providing protection to suffering sentient beings,
one attains the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the feet.
They do not treat sentient beings as strangers;
they harbor no thoughts of robbery or theft;
and toward those worthy of respect, [they act with reverence].
First, one should inquire after their well-being with words, join the palms in reverence,
and make offerings of affectionate thoughts and material wealth,
thereby breaking all forms of pride and arrogance.
One obtains slender, long fingers;
thus, one first attains three marks.
Through karma, one obtains high-arched heels.
Because he gathered in sentient beings through the four means of attraction,
he obtained webbed hands and feet.
Because he was respected by others,
bathing their bodies, assisting them with wash-water, and massaging them,
he obtained the mark of soft and supple hands and feet.
Cultivating all wholesome dharmas without weariness in successive rebirths,
one attains the mark of rounded shoulders.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
Listening to the Dharma with single-minded concentration and expounding the true teaching,
one obtains the antelope-king’s tuft and personally receives the True Dharma.
He extensively expounded [the Dharma] for others and served as a messenger for the sake of the Dharma;
thus he attained the mark of non-protruding ankle bones.
He practices the three types of action in successive stages until they are purified;
he nurses the sick and gives medicine,
remaining free from all forms of pride.
Cultivating contentment,
his hands reach down to his knees;
he beholds those who are separated from one another.
Harmonizing with the Dharma,
one cultivates a sense of shame and dread of blame,
and bestows clothing upon others.
He attains the mark of the horse's sheath;
he purely cultivates the three karmas and also teaches others to cultivate them.
Know moderation in eating and drinking;
provide medicine to the sick;
and take care of those who perform difficult tasks.
Having accumulated rare and precious wealth,
through the balancing of the increases and decreases of the four great elements,
one attains the mark of a perfectly formed body.
Immediately upon ascending, he obtained calves that were round and well-proportioned;
as a result of his karma, the hairs on his body grew upward;
and he cultivated all wholesome dharmas.
Possessing clear and penetrating wisdom,
he contemplates the subtle meanings of all phenomena and shows reverence toward those worthy of honor.
He delights in practicing offerings and embraces his fellow practitioners as virtuous friends.
He was instructed in the meaning [of the teachings] and attained the mark of each hair curling to the right.
He provided him with superior clothing, food, carriages, and ornaments for adorning the body.
By practicing generosity toward all and not giving rise to anger,
one attains the two marks of a golden-hued body and a halo.
Furthermore, because he attained each hair curling to the right,
his skin became soft and supple; and because he extensively bestowed gifts upon sentient beings and established great assemblies for offerings, [he obtained these marks].
Having attained the perfection of the seven parts,
one acts as the leader for all wholesome dharmas, both those already arisen and those yet to arise.
Free from the conceit of "I," he is gentle by nature,
acting thus to eliminate unwholesome states.
He was taught the wholesome dharmas. Consequently,
he obtained the mark of an upper body like that of a lion,
and further obtained the mark of long, slender fingers.

Through the karma of abstaining from divisive speech and reconciling those who are divided, one attains three marks: arms and elbows that are rounded and well-proportioned, the bones of the body are full,
and the body is straight and well-proportioned.
He attains the two marks of having forty teeth that are even and closely set;
he cultivates loving-kindness toward the realm of desire and contemplates the meaning of the Dharma.
He attains white and pure teeth;
he bestows gifts with joy according to the needs of sentient beings;
and he attains square-jawed cheeks.
He bestows the supreme flavor of the Dharma;
for those who have destroyed all flavors,
he purifies their taste.
Attaining the successive stages and the supreme flavor,
one upholds the five precepts and further transmits them to others.
Constantly practicing compassion and dedicating [merit] toward the Great Dharma,
one attains two marks: the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head with the invisible summit, and the broad and long tongue.
By constantly practicing truthful speech, pleasant speech, timely speech, and speech in accordance with the Dharma,
and by skillfully expounding the teachings,
one attains the Brahma-voice.
He practices a mind of universal compassion toward all sentient beings,
just like parents;
he attains the two marks of having deep blue eyes and the ability to blink both the upper and lower eyelids.
One who sees those with true virtue and praises them will obtain the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
The individual causes are thus explained.
Next, the common causes are clarified.
That many marks and signs arise from a single cause is what is termed a "common cause."
Regarding these, two gates are explained as in the *Bhūmivastu* (Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra).
The first concerns the classification according to the four types of cultivation.
As for the definitive cultivation of all wholesome dharmas:
One who practices with single-minded devotion shall obtain the mark of level and well-planted feet;

the mark of thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the feet; the mark of high-arched ankles; the mark of webbed hands and feet; the mark of soft and supple hands and feet; the mark of fullness at seven locations; the mark of full clavicles; the mark of long and rounded arms and elbows; the mark of a straight and well-proportioned body; and the mark of a broad and long tongue—these nine marks.
One who practices constantly attains five marks:
long and slender fingers, high-arched insteps, hands that reach the knees while standing, a well-proportioned body, and teeth that are even and closely set.
One who practices without fault [attains further marks].
One attains the remaining marks.
Second, there is the classification based on the eight kinds of pure karma regarding all sentient beings.
By being free from anger and resentment,
one attains the two marks of having soft hands and feet and fine, delicate skin;
this occurs as one practices in successive stages.
He attains the mark of well-rounded calves;
he makes offerings with the light of joy and offers praise with the sound of virtuous thoughts.
Having attained the four marks— the body golden in color, the halo extending one fathom, teeth white and pure, and the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows—
he felt no joy in his reputation;
he concealed his virtues.
He attains the mark of the horse’s sheath;
he dedicates all roots of goodness cultivated toward enlightenment.
He attains the forty marks: body hairs curling upward, teeth arranged in sequence, the attainment of the supreme sense of taste, and the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head;
through diligent cultivation of vigor, he attains the two marks of the upper body being like that of a lion and the squareness of the jaw.
He pacifies the minds of sentient beings as if looking upon an only son;
he possesses teeth that are even and closely set, eyes that are deep blue and radiant, and the three marks of the upper and lower eyelids blinking.
Cultivating virtue without weariness results in the attainment of other marks;
such is the common cause.
Next, the discussion concerns the universal cause.
Because all characteristics arise from practice without distinction,
it is called the universal cause.
Within this section,
there are three distinctions.
The first provides a general explanation that ethical conduct (*śīla*) serves as the cause.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
the undifferentiated causes for the thirty-two marks are all the observance of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If one does not maintain the precepts,
one cannot even obtain the body of a lowly person,
let alone the marks of a great man.
The second proclaims that the hundred merits serve as the cause.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
each of the thirty-two marks is adorned by one hundred merits.
As for those with a hundred merits,
they practice the ten wholesome deeds within the five grades of mind.
That is to say, the lower, middle, and upper grades, along with the upper-middle and uppermost-upper grades,
constitute fifty. One begins by practicing these fifty and ultimately completes these fifty.
These constitute the hundred blessings.
These hundred are still distinctions within the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Thirdly, this speaks of the causes with respect to all practices.
In truth, according to a general discussion of the principle,
each and every conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*) attains the fruit of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) without any distinction.
The nature of the cause is thus; this concludes the first section.
Next is the second section, which distinguishes [the stages] according to their positions.
In reality, according to the comprehensive discourse,
this extends from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment through to the end of the Cloud of Dharma stage, within each and every bhūmi.
There is nothing that does not fully cultivate the causes for the marks and signs;
according to the completion of these marks,
one dwells within the stages of the happy realms.
Only then does one begin to practice;
having attained the seeds of the lineage (gotra) and above, one dwells within the stage of practice through understanding (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi).
Through skillful means, the fruit is produced;
from the first bhūmi upward,
the attainment of the fruit becomes manifest.
Thus concludes these two sections on the respective positions.
Next is the third section,
which clarifies that the causes for the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) consist of the three immeasurables (trīṇy apramāṇāni), which are capable of producing those marks.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
one kalpa is immeasurable;
it may also be termed "immeasurable time."
From the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) upward,
one practices for three *asaṃkhyeya* great kalpas; therefore,
the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are produced.
Second, through the two immeasurables of mind—
bringing peace and happiness and benefiting all sentient beings—
one gives rise to the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence.
The three types of conduct are immeasurable;
there is no wholesome karma that he does not fully cultivate.
Thus, the three gates concerning the production of the primary and secondary marks are concluded.
Next is the fourth gate, which clarifies the differences between what is taught in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; this consists of eleven sub-sections.
First, regarding the distinction by realm:
the followers of the Mahāyāna say that these are the causes of the marks and signs of physical perfection.
Nāgārjuna taught that this cultivation belongs only to the desire realm and not to the two higher realms; however, he also stated that it is cultivated in both the desire and form realms.
It is not the case that this does not apply to the formless realm; the principle extends to it as well,
because all wholesome karma is capable of producing the causes for the primary and secondary marks.
Second, the classification according to the realms of rebirth (*gati*).
The followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) say that it is cultivated among human beings.
Nāgārjuna taught that this applies to all five realms of existence,
such as the case of Sāgara, the Dragon King, and others like him.
All these are bodhisattvas practicing together the causes for Buddhahood.
Third, distinguishing by way of location,
it is taught within the Hīnayāna.
Nāgārjuna taught that cultivation occurs in Jambudvīpa and not in other regions;
among the three continents, it excludes Uttarakuru.
This principle also applies universally:
because a bodhisattva is omnipresent in all places,
their cultivation is entirely capable of serving as the cause for the primary and secondary marks.
Fourth, regarding the classification by way of the body:
it is taught in the Hīnayāna that [the path] is cultivated by those with male or female bodies.
Nāgārjuna stated that even those such as eunuchs are able to practice;
this is explained in detail in the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā*.
In the Hīnayāna it is taught that [this practice] is cultivated solely in the mind and does not extend to the body or speech;
this is one point.
Nāgārjuna does not refute the principle that [merit] pervades the three types of action;
for all wholesome acts such as prostration and praise are entirely capable of serving as causes for the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha.
Sixth, regarding the analysis according to consciousness:
the Hinayana proclaims that it is cultivated within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Nāgārjuna’s teaching is the "teaching of penetration.
The seventh [category], the "many and small distinctions," is taught within the Hīnayāna.
For each of those individual marks, a single volition serves as the primary cause,
while many volitions act as auxiliary factors to bring it to completion;
this was proclaimed by Nāgārjuna.
Regarding each individual mark,
it takes immeasurable thoughts as its cause.
This is analyzed according to eight temporal aspects.
In the Hīnayāna it is said that one practices when a Buddha has appeared in the world,
but does not practice at other times.
Nāgārjuna taught that one should practice at all times;
this is explained in nine ways according to the distinctions of the stages.
In the Hīnayāna it is said that a bodhisattva completes three asaṃkhyeya kalpas and, separately during one hundred kalpas,
cultivates the karma for the marks and signs of physical perfection.
The minimum duration for cultivation is ninety-one kalpas,
as in the case of Śākyamuni Buddha;
this was proclaimed by Nāgārjuna.
From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until Buddhahood, one constantly cultivates this;
it is categorized according to its objects as tenfold,
as explained in the Hīnayāna.
Cultivation based on the Buddha’s body;
this is the general teaching as explained by Nāgārjuna.
This concludes the sequential analysis of the eleventh gate.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
some proclaim that one first cultivates the mark of level soles under the feet.
One must first establish the foundation before being able to give rise to the others.
Alternatively, some say that one first cultivates the Tathāgata’s mark of deep blue eyes.
Because one gazes upon sentient beings with compassion by means of this mark of the eyes, one cultivates it first;
Nāgārjuna refutes this.
The explanation of cultivation is not in sequential order.
The above was the second section, clarifying the causes of the marks and signs;
next is the third gate.
The practice of cultivation is clarified;
in reality, the principle applies equally to both, yet they are provisionally distinguished according to their respective meanings.
One cultivates the various marks in order to purify the vessel of the body and to embrace the pure dharmas of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
just as one who wishes to invite a king first adorns his residence.
Just as one who desires excellent food first prepares precious vessels,
so it is here. As it is said in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
This constitutes self-benefit.
Cultivating the various marks of excellence is for the purpose of gathering sentient beings, causing them to give rise to love, respect, and joy in what is taught.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that worldly sentient beings take refuge in the eighty deities and Buddhas for their protection; therefore,
one should cultivate the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
These eighty deities are as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* among the ten virtues;
their marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are likewise.
The four types of universal purity are:
purity of body, purity of mind, purity of objective sphere, and purity of wisdom.
Their meaning is as explained above.
Regarding these ten powers (daśabala),
from the power of the possible and impossible up to the power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya),
their meaning is as explained above.
Now, following the sūtra, I shall briefly distinguish its characteristics.
The sūtra states that the first power consists of nine phrases.
First, the Tathāgata distinguishes the individual qualities of persons.
As explained in the *Bhūmivastu-vyākhyā*,
he is called the Tathāgata because the speech he utters does not deviate from suchness (*tathatā*).
Second, regarding "place and non-place" (*sthānāsthāna*), this refers to the scope of his power.
Because pure and impure fruits depend upon specific causes, these are called "possible" (sthāna);
because they contradict specific causes, they are called "impossible" (asthāna).
The power of these consists in the three kinds of knowledge as they truly are.
As explained in the *Bhūmivastu-vyākhyā*,
knowledge free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) is not merely the absence of ignorance followed by a false claim to knowledge; rather,
it is the fourth [point], which establishes the meaning of the term "power" (*bala*).
As explained in the *Bhūmivastu-vyākhyā*,
the power of self-conduct (*svayaṃ-caryā-bala*) consists in attaining victory by relinquishing all māras;
this is what is termed "power."
The capacity to benefit all sentient beings is called "power" (*bala*);
it is the power of transforming others.
Fifth, the accomplishment [of the result] distinguishes the result from its cause.
As explained in the *Bhūmivastu-vyākhyā*,
it is called "accomplishment" because one cultivates and masters [the perfections] so as to attain sovereignty according to one's will.
The power of mastery through cultivation is accomplished;
the sovereign power of action according to one's will is accomplished.
Sixth, the manifestation of supreme excellence signifies the perfection of the fruit.
Unsurpassed nirvāṇa is called "supreme and wondrous.
Seventh, "tranquility" manifests the ripening of its cause:
the attainment of the Eightfold Noble Path.
It is called "peaceful" because it is far removed from all afflictions, disturbances, and fears.
Eighth, it is able to turn the Brahma-wheel.
Ninth, it is able to roar the lion’s roar.
The transformative benefit of these two powers for virtuous persons is called "turning the Brahma-wheel" because it removes afflictions and attains tranquility;
it is called "the lion’s roar" because it subdues the assemblies of the heterodox and causes them to abandon divergent views.
Among these nine, the first seven constitute the path for one's own peace,
while the latter two constitute the peace of others.
The second is the power of karma.
The sūtra contains seven statements.
The first is knowing the karma of the three periods of time.
Second, he knows the three types of karma: those of body, speech, and mind.
Third, he knows the four modes of karmic retribution (*dharmasamādāna*):
there are phenomena that are painful in the present but bring happiness later.
There are phenomena that are pleasant in the present but painful in the future; there are phenomena that are painful both in the present and in the future;
and there are phenomena that are pleasant both in the present and in the future.
As extensively analyzed in the treatise, these are the four types of acceptance of dharmas (*dharmasamādāna*).
Fourth, knowing the number of sentient beings who act as the agents of karma.
Fifth, knowing the objective spheres (*gocara*) of karma created by both sentient and non-sentient beings.
Sixth, knowing the causes of karma;
seventh, knowing the fruits of karma.
There are two types of concentration power.
First, it clarifies how the Tathāgata possesses mastery over meditative concentration and manifests various transformations;
second, it clarifies how he knows whether the concentrated minds of sentient beings exist or not,
and accordingly teaches them to practice according to their capacity.
Knowing the inferior, middling, and superior faculties of other sentient beings is called the power of the faculties (*indriyabala*).
Knowing the inferior, middling, and superior inclinations of other sentient beings is called the power of inclination (*chandasbala*).
Knowing the differences in the dispositions for the three vehicles and the various natures of the afflictions of other sentient beings [is called the power of resolve].
This is called the power of nature (*dharmatā-bala*).

It consists in knowing the various gates of the perfections (*pāramitā*) to instruct sentient beings, as well as knowing the various differing views of sentient beings and their respective destinations; this is called the path leading to those destinations (*yathāgati-mārga*).
Knowing the eight kinds of matters and the six kinds of associated practices of past lives is called the power of recollecting former existences (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*).
These eight kinds of matters and six kinds of associated practices have been fully explained as before.
As for the power of the divine eye:
the Tathāgata’s divine eye is purified and surpasses that of humans;
with it, he sees all sentient beings, whether they possess beautiful forms or ugly forms.
Furthermore, one sees sentient beings— through their wholesome or unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind— at the dissolution of the body after death,
either being reborn in a happy realm or falling into an evil destiny.
This is the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
The Tathāgata has completely exhausted all his own outflows and is endowed with all virtues;
he also knows which sentient beings have exhausted [their defilements] and which have not.
He provides instruction according to what is appropriate;
such is the nature of the Ten Powers.
As for the Four Fearlessnesses:
This refers to all-knowledge up to the ability to teach the path that leads to the exhaustion of suffering;
the meaning is as explained above.
As for the three foundations of mindfulness:
The Tathāgata has long cherished the thought that my Dharma is the most supreme;
yet, toward those who accept it and those who do not,
he does not give rise to a mind of resentment.
There are three kinds of assemblies:
first, the orthodox assembly;
second, the heterodox assembly.
Third, that which is neither right nor wrong.
Regarding these three classes of beings,
one should maintain a mind of right mindfulness.
Without increase or decrease,
these are called the three foundations of mindfulness.
As for the three ways in which he needs no protection:
The Buddha has forever exhausted all karma of body, speech, and mind, such that there is no need for protection;
this is called the "three non-protections.
As for what is termed "great compassion":
The four immeasurable minds are collectively termed "great compassion.
Regarding the one who does not forget the Dharma:
the Tathāgata, with respect to those [beings'] body, speech, and mind, etc.,...
To constantly keep in mind and never forget the tasks that ought to be performed is called the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asampramoṣadharma*).
This refers to one who has severed all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The Tathāgata’s movements, postures, gazes, and speech are free from all residual habitual tendencies arising from afflictions;
this is called the severance of all habits.
This is the one who possesses the sublime wisdom of all modes.
The Buddha knows three dharmas:
first, that which is beneficial in meaning is a wholesome dharma;
second, that which is not beneficial in meaning is an unwholesome dharma.
The third is that which is neither meaningful nor meaningless;
it is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomenon. Because it differs from the preceding two, it is called "neither meaningful nor meaningless. Among these three:
Knowing the unwholesome and the indeterminate is called the knowledge of all modes;
knowing wholesome dharmas is called wondrous wisdom.
These two combined are designated as the knowledge of all modes.
The differentiation of the one hundred and forty dharmas is thus.
Next, the second section clarifies their functions;
these are the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
There are ten kinds of activities for benefiting sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions. First,
desiring to cause sentient beings to purify their faith and receive the body of a great man, he gives rise to the various marks and signs of excellence.
Second, for the sake of performing all activities without obstruction and with mastery, one brings about the four kinds of purity in every respect.
Third, for the benefit of sentient beings, one eliminates all doubts by bringing forth the ten powers of a Buddha.
Fourth, to open up the Tathāgata’s all-knowing vision to answer all questions,
to subdue all heterodox arguments, to establish the correct doctrine, and to give rise to the four fearlessnesses; fifth,
for the Tathāgata’s wisdom to discipline and transform sentient beings.
According to the various sentient beings,
whether they abide or do not abide within the True Dharma.
He does not give rise to a mind of affliction;
he gives rise to the three applications of mindfulness; and in all his actions, there is no fault.
He gives rise to the three kinds of non-protection.
Seventh, he constantly observes the world with the Buddha-eye and gives rise to a heart of great compassion.
Eighth, because all that was to be done for sentient beings has already been accomplished, he gives rise to the quality of non-forgetfulness.
Ninth, the conduct of the Tathāgata accords with suchness (tathatā) and is free from any remaining fault.
He gives rise to the abandonment of all habitual tendencies.
He completely distances himself from the ten unwholesome paths and the indeterminate; he analytically elucidates all wholesome dharmas.
Therefore, he gives rise to the wondrous wisdom of all modes.
The functions are thus.
Next is the third section,
which correlates and subsumes these under the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) have been extensively explained above. Among those eighteen,
three refer to the absence of error in the three types of action (*trividha-karma*), and three refer to the three types of action being in accordance with wisdom (*jñānānuparivartin*).
Among the one hundred and forty [unwholesome states], three are subsumed under the "three kinds of non-protection.
Regarding those without divergent thoughts:
toward all sentient beings.
Abiding in a mind of equanimity, one has no perception of enemy or friend.
This is subsumed under three of the fourteen types of mindfulness;
there is no lack of concentration.
Among the one hundred and forty [mental states], those subsumed under the power of concentration are all characterized by equanimity born of full knowledge;
among the one hundred and forty, those subsumed under the non-forgetfulness of the Dharma are likewise so characterized.
His wisdom does not diminish, nor do his knowledge and vision diminish;
he thoroughly penetrates the three periods of time,
encompassed by the sublime knowledge of all modes within the one hundred and forty [qualities].
Liberation is without decrease.
Among the one hundred and forty [factors], all habitual tendencies are subsumed.
Within those eighteen, the three—desire, mindfulness, and diligence—are without decrease.
Among these one hundred and forty [qualities],

the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, the four types of purity in all aspects, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and great compassion are briefly mentioned without further elaboration.
Among those eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), some are concealed and not manifested;
the Buddha’s virtues are immeasurable, with the hidden and the manifest being presented alternately,
so that one cannot demand full enumeration of them all.
The one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) have been briefly elucidated in this manner.
